{{Short description|Arctangent function with two arguments}}
{{lowercase title}}
[[File:Atan2 differs from arctan.png|thumb|{{math|atan2(''y'', ''x'')}} returns the angle {{mvar|θ}} between the positive {{mvar|x}}-axis and the [[ray (geometry)|ray]] from the origin to the point {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}}, confined to {{open-closed|−''π'', ''π''}}.]]
[[File:Arctangent2.svg|thumb|Graph of <math>\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)</math> over <math>y / x</math>]]

In [[computing]] and [[mathematics]], the [[function (mathematics)|function]] '''atan2''' is the 2-[[Argument of a function|argument]] [[arctangent]]. By definition, <math>\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)</math> is the [[angle measure]] (in [[radian]]s, with <math>-\pi < \theta \leq \pi</math>) between the positive [[Cartesian coordinate system|<math>x</math>-axis]] and the [[ray (geometry)|ray]] from the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]] to the point <math>(x,\,y)</math> in the [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian plane]]. Equivalently, <math>\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)</math> is the [[argument (complex analysis)|argument]] (also called ''phase'' or ''angle'') of the [[complex number]] <math>x + iy.</math> (The ''argument'' of a function and the ''argument'' of a complex number, each mentioned above, should not be confused.)

The <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math> function first appeared in the programming language [[Fortran]] in 1961. It was originally intended to return a correct and unambiguous value for the angle {{tmath|\theta}} in converting from Cartesian coordinates {{tmath|(x,\,y)}} to [[polar coordinates]] {{tmath|(r,\,\theta)}}. If <math>\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)</math> and <math display=inline>r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}</math>, then <math>x = r \cos \theta</math> and <math>y = r \sin \theta.</math>

If {{tmath|x > 0}}, the desired angle measure is <math display=inline>\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) = \arctan\left( y / x \right).</math> However, when {{math|''x'' < 0}}, the angle <math>\arctan(y / x)</math> is [[antipodal point|diametrically opposite]] the desired angle, and {{tmath|\pm\pi}} (a half [[turn (angle)|turn]]) must be added to place the point in the correct [[quadrant (plane geometry)|quadrant]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://scipp.ucsc.edu/~haber/ph116A/arg_11.pdf|title=The argument of a complex number|date=Winter 2011|publisher=Santa Cruz Institute for Particle Physics}}</ref> Using the <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math> function does away with this correction, simplifying code and mathematical formulas.

== Motivation ==
It is common in practical applications of geometry to convert between [[rectangular coordinates]] {{tmath|(x, y)}} and [[polar coordinates]] {{tmath|(r, \theta)}} for representing points in the [[Euclidean plane]], for example to find the [[signed angle]] representing the [[Orientation (geometry)|orientation]] of a [[Euclidean vector|vector]] or to calculate the [[Argument (complex analysis)|argument]] of a [[complex number]]. The relationships between rectangular and polar coordinates can be summarized by the equations:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
x &= r\cos\theta, & \qquad r &= {\textstyle \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} }, \\[2pt]
y &= r\sin\theta, & \tan\theta &= \frac{y}{x},
\end{align}</math>
where {{tmath|\sin}}, {{tmath|\cos}}, and {{tmath|\tan}} are [[trigonometric functions]] and {{tmath|\textstyle \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} }} is the [[Pythagorean addition|Pythagorean sum]] of {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}}, i.e. the [[hypotenuse]] of a [[right triangle]] with legs {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}}.

[[File:Atan2 argument sign graph.svg|thumb|Graph of the tangent function from {{math|−''π''}} to {{math|+''π''}} with the corresponding signs of {{math|''y''/''x''}}. The green arrows point to the results of {{math|atan2(−1,&nbsp;−1)}} and {{math|atan2(1,&nbsp;1)}}.]]
Computing {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} from {{tmath|r}} and {{tmath|\theta}} directly from these formulas is straightforward. In the other direction, though, it is helpful to provide special functions to implement the conversions. The formula to compute {{tmath|r}} from {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} can lead to numerical overflows and underflows, avoided by the <code>hypot</code> function of many standard libraries. The computation of {{tmath|\theta}} from {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} is more complicated, for two reasons: (1) because it could involve a division by zero and (2) because the quotient {{tmath|y / x}} is equal to  {{tmath|(-y) / (-x)}}, and therefore does not distinguish between point {{tmath|(x, y)}} and the opposite point {{tmath|(-x, -y)}}. The ordinary single-argument [[arctangent]] function only returns angle measures in the interval {{tmath|\left({-\tfrac12\pi}, \tfrac12\pi\right) }}, so a naïve implementation of a conversion from rectangular to polar coordinates, {{tmath|1= \theta = \arctan(y / x)}}, will yield incorrect results whenever {{tmath|x \le 0}}.

To fully determine the direction angle from the origin given a point {{tmath|(x,\,y)}} using the arctangent function, mathematical formulas or computer code must handle multiple cases; at least one for positive values of <math>x</math> and one for negative values of {{tmath|x}}, and sometimes additional cases when {{tmath|y}} is negative or one coordinate is zero.

To save programmers the trouble, computer [[programming language]]s introduced the {{math|atan2}} function, at least as early as the [[Fortran]] IV language of the 1960s.<ref>{{Cite book
 | last = Organick
 | first = Elliott I.
 | year =1966
 | title = A FORTRAN IV Primer
 | publisher = Addison-Wesley
 | quote = Some processors also offer the library function called ATAN2, a function of two arguments (opposite and adjacent).
 | pages = 42
}}</ref> The quantity {{tmath|\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)}} is the angle measure between the {{tmath|x}}-axis and a ray from the origin to a point {{tmath|(x,\,y)}} anywhere in the Cartesian plane. The [[sign (mathematics)|signs]] of {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} are used to determine the [[quadrant (plane geometry)|quadrant]] of the result and select the correct branch of the [[multivalued function]] {{tmath|\operatorname{Arctan}(y/x)}}.

The {{math|atan2}} function is useful in many applications involving [[Euclidean vector]]s, such as finding the direction from one point to another or converting a [[rotation matrix]] to [[Euler angle]]s.

The {{math|atan2}} function is now included in many other programming languages, and is also commonly found in mathematical formulas throughout science and engineering.

=== Argument order ===

In 1961, Fortran introduced the {{math|atan2}} function with argument order {{tmath|(y, x)}} so that the [[argument (complex analysis)|argument]] (phase angle) of a complex number is <math>\operatorname{arg}z = \operatorname{atan2}(\operatorname{Im}z, \operatorname{Re}z).</math> This follows the left-to-right order of a fraction written <math>y / x,</math> so that <math>\operatorname{atan2}(y, x) = \operatorname{atan}(y / x)</math> for positive values of <math>x.</math> However, this is the opposite of the conventional component order for complex numbers, <math>z = x + iy,</math> or as coordinates <math>(\operatorname{Re}z, \operatorname{Im}z).</math> See section [[#Definition and computation|Definition and computation]].

Some other programming languages (see § [[#Realizations of the function in common computer languages|Realizations of the function in common computer languages]]) picked the opposite order instead. For example, [[Microsoft Excel]] uses <math>\operatorname{Atan2}(x,\,y),</math> [[Apache OpenOffice#Calc|OpenOffice Calc]] uses <math>\operatorname{arctan2}(x,\,y),</math> and [[Mathematica]] uses <math>\operatorname{ArcTan}[x,y],</math> defaulting to one-argument arctangent if called with one argument.

== <span class="anchor" id="Definition"></span> Definition and computation ==
The function {{math|atan2}} computes the [[principal value|principal]] [[argument (complex analysis)|argument]] of the [[complex number]] {{tmath|x + iy}}, which is also the imaginary part of the principal value of the [[complex logarithm]]. That is,
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\operatorname{atan2}(y, x) &= \operatorname{arg}(x + iy)\\
&= \operatorname{Im}\operatorname{log}(x + iy).
\end{align}</math>

Adding any [[integer]] multiple of {{tmath|2\pi}} (corresponding to complete turns around the origin) gives another argument of the same complex number, but the principal argument is defined as the unique representative angle in the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{tmath|( -\pi, \pi ]}}.

In terms of the standard arctangent function, whose image is {{tmath|\left({-\tfrac12\pi}, \tfrac12\pi\right)}}, {{math|atan2}} can be expressed [[piecewise-defined function|piecewise]]:
<math display="block"> \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) =
\begin{cases}
 \arctan\left(\frac y x\right) &\text{if } x > 0, \\[5mu]
 \arctan\left(\frac y x\right) + \pi &\text{if } x < 0 \text{ and } y \ge 0, \\[5mu]
 \arctan\left(\frac y x\right) - \pi &\text{if } x < 0 \text{ and } y < 0, \\[5mu]
 +\frac{\pi}{2} &\text{if } x = 0 \text{ and } y > 0, \\[5mu]
 -\frac{\pi}{2} &\text{if } x = 0 \text{ and } y < 0, \\[5mu]
 \text{undefined} &\text{if } x = 0 \text{ and } y = 0.
\end{cases}</math>

[[File:The principal value of the argument (-atan2- in some circles).svg|thumb|The tangent of half an angle can be computed in terms of coordinates {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} and radius {{mvar|r}}.]]

In cases where the {{math|atan2}} function is unavailable or inconvenient to use, and where reducing the number of cases that must be considered is important (e.g. for [[Array programming|vectorized computations]] on a GPU), it can be useful to compute {{math|atan2}} through a [[tangent half-angle formula]]:<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kusaka |first1=Takashi |last2=Tanaka |first2=Takayuki |title=Fast and accurate approximation methods for trigonometric and arctangent calculations for low-performance computers |journal=Electronics |volume=11 |number=15 |year=2022 |article-number=2285}}</ref>

<math display=block>
\operatorname{atan2}(y, x) = 2 \arctan \left(\frac{y}{\textstyle \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} + x}\right),
</math>
except in the case that {{tmath|x < 0}} and {{tmath|1=y = 0}}, when by convention atan2 is equal to {{tmath|\pi}}.

== Derivative ==
{{details|Winding number}}
As the function {{math|atan2}} is a function of two variables, it has two [[partial derivative]]s. At points where these derivatives exist, {{math|atan2}} is, except for a constant, equal to {{math|arctan(''y''/''x'')}}. Hence,
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
& \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\operatorname{atan2}(y,\, x) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \arctan\left(\frac y x \right) = -\frac{y}{x^2 + y^2}, \\[5pt]
& \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\operatorname{atan2}(y,\, x) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \arctan\left(\frac y x \right) = \frac x {x^2 + y^2}.
\end{align}
</math>
These two partial derivatives are the coordinates of the [[gradient]].

Informally representing the function {{math|atan2}} as the angle function {{math|1=''θ''(''x'', ''y'') = atan2(''y'', ''x'')}} (which is only defined up to a constant) yields the following formula for the [[total differential]]:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\operatorname{atan2}(y,\, x)\,\mathrm{d}x + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\operatorname{atan2}(y,\, x)\,\mathrm{d}y \\[5pt]
&= -\frac{y}{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm{d}x + \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm{d}y.
\end{align}</math>

While the function {{math|atan2}} is discontinuous along the negative {{mvar|x}}-axis, reflecting the fact that angle cannot be continuously defined, this derivative is continuously defined except at the origin, reflecting the fact that [[infinitesimal]] (and indeed local) ''changes'' in angle can be defined everywhere except the origin. Integrating this derivative along a path gives the total change in angle over the path, and integrating over a closed loop gives the [[winding number]].

In the language of [[differential geometry]], this derivative is a [[one-form]], and it is [[closed differential form|closed]] (its derivative is zero) but not [[exact differential form|exact]] (it is not the derivative of a 0-form, i.e., a function), and in fact it generates the first [[de Rham cohomology]] of the [[punctured plane]]. This is the most basic example of such a form, and it is fundamental in differential geometry.

The partial derivatives of {{math|atan2}} do not contain [[trigonometric functions]], making it particularly useful in many applications (e.g. embedded systems) where trigonometric functions can be expensive to evaluate.

The diagram uses the standard mathematical convention that angles increase [[Clockwise|counterclockwise]] from zero along the ray to the right. Note that the order of arguments is reversed; the function {{math|atan2(''y'', ''x'')}} computes the angle corresponding to the point {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}}.

[[File:Atan2atan.png|thumb|right|300px|Comparison of [[Inverse trigonometric functions|arctan]] and atan2 functions]]
This figure shows the values of <math>\arctan(\tan(\theta))</math> along with <math>\operatorname {atan2}(\sin(\theta),\cos(\theta))</math> for <math>0\le \theta \le 2\pi</math>. Both functions are odd and periodic with periods <math>\pi</math> and <math>2\pi</math>, respectively, and thus can easily be supplemented to any region of real values of <math>\theta</math>. One can clearly see the [[branch cut]]s of the <math>\operatorname {atan2}</math>-function at <math>\theta = \pi</math>, and of the <math>\arctan</math>-function at <math>\theta \in \bigl\{\tfrac{\pi}{2},\;\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\bigr\}</math>.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mndynamics.com/indexp.html|title=Wolf Jung: Mandel, software for complex dynamics|website=www.mndynamics.com|access-date=20 April 2018}}</ref>

== Angle sum and difference identity ==
{{Main|List of trigonometric identities#Angle sum and difference identities}}

The sum or difference of multiple angles to be computed by {{tmath|\operatorname{atan2} }} can alternately be computed by composing them as [[complex number]]s. Given two coordinate pairs {{tmath|(x_1, y_1)}} and {{tmath|(x_2, y_2)}}, their angles from the positive {{tmath|x}} axis will be composed (and lengths multiplied) if they are treated as complex numbers and then multiplied together, {{tmath|1=(x_1 + iy_1)(x_2 + iy_2)={} }}{{tmath|(x_1x_2 - y_1y_2) + i(y_1x_2 + x_1y_2)}}. The resulting angle can be found using a single {{tmath|\operatorname{atan2} }} operation, so long as the resulting angle lies in {{tmath|(-\pi, \pi]}}:
<math display="block">
\operatorname{atan2} (y_1, x_1) \pm \operatorname{atan2} (y_2, x_2) = \operatorname{atan2} (y_1 x_2 \pm x_1 y_2, x_1 x_2 \mp y_1 y_2),
</math>
and likewise for more than two coordinate pairs. If the composed angle crosses the negative {{tmath|x}}-axis (i.e. exceeds the range {{tmath|(-\pi, \pi]}}), then the crossings can be counted and the appropriate integer multiple of {{tmath|2\pi}} added to the final result to correct it.

This difference formula is frequently used in practice to compute the angle between two planar [[Euclidean vector|vector]]s, since the resulting angle is always in the range {{tmath|(-\pi, \pi]}}.

== East-counterclockwise, north-clockwise and south-clockwise conventions, etc. ==

The <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math> function was originally designed for the convention in pure mathematics that can be termed ''east-counterclockwise''. In practical applications, however, the ''north-clockwise'' and ''south-clockwise'' conventions are often the norm. In atmospheric sciences, for instance, the [[wind direction]] can be calculated using the <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math> function with the east- and north-components of the wind vector as its arguments;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eol.ucar.edu/content/wind-direction-quick-reference|title=Wind Direction Quick Reference|publisher=NCAR UCAR Earth Observing Laboratory}}</ref> the [[solar azimuth angle]] can be calculated similarly with the east- and north-components of the solar vector as its arguments. The wind direction is normally defined in the north-clockwise sense, and the solar azimuth angle uses both the north-clockwise and south-clockwise conventions widely.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.renene.2021.03.047|title=A solar azimuth formula that renders circumstantial treatment unnecessary without compromising mathematical rigor: Mathematical setup, application and extension of a formula based on the subsolar point and atan2 function|year=2021|last1=Zhang|first1=Taiping|last2=Stackhouse|first2=Paul W.|last3=MacPherson|first3=Bradley|last4=Mikovitz|first4=J. Colleen|journal=Renewable Energy|volume=172|pages=1333–1340|s2cid=233631040|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021REne..172.1333Z }}</ref> These different conventions can be realized by swapping the positions and changing the signs of the {{mvar|x}}- and {{mvar|y}}-arguments as follows:
* <math>\operatorname{atan2}(y,\,x),\;\;\;\;\;</math> (East-Counterclockwise Convention)
* <math>\operatorname{atan2}(x,\,y),\;\;\;\;\;</math> (North-Clockwise Convention)
* <math>\operatorname{atan2}({-x},\,{-y})</math>. (South-Clockwise Convention)

As an example, let <math display="inline">x_{0}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}</math> and <math display="inline">y_{0}=\frac{1}{2}</math>, then the east-counterclockwise format gives <math display="inline">\operatorname{atan2}(y_{0}, x_{0})\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=30^{\circ}</math>, the north-clockwise format gives <math display="inline">\operatorname{atan2}(x_{0}, y_{0})\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=60^{\circ}</math>, and the south-clockwise format gives <math display="inline">\operatorname{atan2}(-x_{0}, -y_{0})\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=-120^{\circ}</math>.

Changing the sign of the {{mvar|x}}- and/or {{mvar|y}}-arguments and/or swapping their positions can create 8 possible variations of the <math>\operatorname{atan2}</math> function and they, interestingly, correspond to 8 possible definitions of the angle, namely, clockwise or counterclockwise starting from each of the 4 [[cardinal direction]]s, north, east, south and west.

== Realizations of the function in common computer languages ==
The realization of the function differs from one computer language to another.

The <math>(\operatorname{Re}, \operatorname{Im})</math> convention (reversed relative to the convention used in the discussion above) is used by:
* In [[Microsoft Excel]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://msdn2.microsoft.com/en-us/library/bb238940.aspx|title=Microsoft Excel Atan2 Method|date=14 June 2014 |publisher=Microsoft}}</ref> [[OpenOffice.org Calc]], [[LibreOffice Calc]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://help.libreoffice.org/Calc/Mathematical_Functions#ATAN2|title=LibreOffice Calc ATAN2|publisher=Libreoffice.org}}</ref> [[Google Docs|Google Spreadsheets]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://support.google.com/docs/topic/1361471 |title=Functions and formulas – Docs Editors Help|website=support.google.com}}</ref> and [[Numbers (spreadsheet)|iWork Numbers]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.apple.com/mac/numbers/compatibility/functions.html#trigonometric |title=Numbers' Trigonometric Function List|publisher=Apple }}</ref> the 2-argument arctangent function has the two arguments in the standard sequence <math>(\operatorname{Re}, \operatorname{Im})</math>.
* In [[Mathematica]], the form <code>ArcTan[''x'',''y'']</code> is used where the one parameter form supplies the normal arctangent. Mathematica classifies <code>ArcTan[0,0]</code> as an indeterminate expression.
* On most TI graphing calculators (excluding the [[TI-85]] and [[TI-86]]), the equivalent function is called '''R►Pθ''' and has the arguments <math>(\operatorname{Re}, \operatorname{Im})</math>.
* On TI-85 the {{math|arg}} function is called <code>angle(x,y)</code> and although it appears to take two arguments, it really only has one complex argument which is denoted by a pair of numbers: {{math|''x'' + ''iy'' {{=}} (''x'', ''y'')}}.

The <math>(\operatorname{Im}, \operatorname{Re})</math> convention is used by:
* The C function <code>atan2</code>, and most other computer implementations, are designed to reduce the effort of transforming cartesian to polar coordinates and so always define <code>atan2(0, 0)</code>. On implementations without [[signed zero]], or when given positive zero arguments, it is normally defined as 0. It will always return a value in the range {{closed-closed|−''π'', ''π''}} rather than raising an error or returning a [[NaN]] (Not a Number).
* In [[Common Lisp]], where optional arguments exist, the <code>atan</code> function allows one to optionally supply the {{mvar|x}} coordinate: <code>(atan&nbsp;''y''&nbsp;''x'')</code>.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/f_asin_.htm|title=CLHS: Function ASIN, ACOS, ATAN|publisher=LispWorks}}</ref>
* In [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]], the situation is similar to Common Lisp: instead of <code>atan2</code>, the language has a one-parameter and a two-parameter form for <code>atan</code>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/base/math/|title=Mathematics · The Julia Language|website=docs.julialang.org}}</ref> However, it has many more than two methods, to allow for aggressive optimisation at [[compile time]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/faq/|title=Frequently Asked Questions · The Julia Language|website=docs.julialang.org}}</ref>
* [[Mathcad]] uses the argument order <code>atan2(x, y)</code>. <code>atan2(0, 0)</code> is undefined.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://support.ptc.com/help/mathcad/r11.0/en/#page/PTC_Mathcad_Help/polar_angles.html|title=Mathcad help - Polar Angles|publisher=PTC}}</ref>
* For systems implementing [[signed zero]], [[Infinity|infinities]], or [[Not a Number]] (for example, [[IEEE floating point]]), it is common to implement reasonable extensions that may extend the range of values produced to include {{math|−''π''}} and −0 when {{math|''y'' {{=}} −0}}. These also may return NaN or raise an exception when given a NaN argument.
* In the [[X86|Intel x86 Architecture]] [[assembler code]], <code>atan2</code> is known as the <code>FPATAN</code> (floating-point partial arctangent) instruction.<ref>IA-32 Intel Architecture Software Developer’s Manual. Volume 2A: Instruction Set Reference, A-M, 2004.</ref> It can deal with infinities and results lie in the closed interval {{closed-closed|−''π'', ''π''}}, e.g. <code>atan2(∞, ''x'')</code> = {{math|+''π''/2}} for finite {{mvar|x}}. Particularly, <code>FPATAN</code> is defined when both arguments are zero:{{Bulleted list
|1= <code>atan2(+0, +0)</code> = +0;
|2= <code>atan2(+0, −0)</code> = {{math|+''π''}};
|3= <code>atan2(−0, +0)</code> = −0;
|4= <code>atan2(−0, −0)</code> = {{math|−''π''}}.
}}{{pb}}This definition is related to the concept of [[signed zero]].
* In mathematical writings other than [[source code]], such as in books and articles, the notations '''Arctan'''<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2LIMMD9FVXkC&q=four+quadrant+inverse+tangent+mathematical+notation&pg=PA234|title=Principles of Digital Image Processing: Fundamental Techniques|first1=Wilhelm|last1=Burger|first2=Mark J.|last2=Burge|date=7 July 2010|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-84800-191-6|access-date=20 April 2018|via=Google Books}}</ref> and '''Tan<sup>−1</sup>'''<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7nNjaH9B0_0C&q=four+quadrant+inverse+tangent+mathematical+notation&pg=PA345|title=Introduction to Circuit Analysis and Design|first=Tildon H.|last=Glisson|date=18 February 2011|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9789048194438|access-date=20 April 2018|via=Google Books}}</ref> have been utilized; these are capitalized variants of the [[Inverse trigonometric functions#Notation|regular]] arctan and tan<sup>−1</sup>. This usage is consistent with the [[complex argument#Notation|complex argument notation]], such that {{math|Atan(''y'', ''x'') {{=}} Arg(''x'' + ''iy'')}}.
* On [[Hewlett-Packard|HP]] calculators, treat the coordinates as a complex number and then take the <code>ARG</code>. Or <code><< C->R ARG >> 'ATAN2' STO</code>.
* On scientific calculators, the function can often be calculated as the angle given when {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} is converted from [[rectangular coordinates]] to [[polar coordinates]].
* Systems supporting symbolic mathematics normally return an undefined value for {{math|atan2(0, 0)}} or otherwise signal that an abnormal condition has arisen.
* The free math library FDLIBM (Freely Distributable LIBM) available from [[netlib]] has source code showing how it implements <code>atan2</code>, including handling the various IEEE exceptional values.
* For systems without a hardware multiplier, the function {{math|atan2}} can be implemented in a numerically reliable manner by the [[CORDIC]] method. Thus, implementations of {{math|atan(''y'')}} will probably choose to compute {{math|atan2(''y'', 1)}}.
